source: Parab, Lu, Wu, Gulwani (2025) Analysis of Error Sources in LLM-based Hypothesis Search for Few-Shot Rule Induction
finding: Re-ran the Wang et al. hypothesis-search pipeline with GPT-4o on 100 list functions and scored each stage. A correct hypothesis existed after generation in under half of trials, and the summarising step threw away a quarter of the correct ones.
numbers: 100 tasks, 11 trials each, 5 runs. Generator (64 samples) had a correct hypothesis in 46.4% of trials; after the summariser cut 64 to 8, 34.5%. Summariser discarded 26% of correct hypotheses (74% kept), costing 12.1 points. Test solve rate 62.0%. Mean test accuracy: hypothesis search .487, humans .521, direct GPT-4o .359, Codex .322.
quote: the Summarizer discards 26% of correct generator hypotheses, retaining only 74%
limits: One model (GPT-4o), one domain (list functions), correctness of hypotheses judged by an LLM evaluator against a text description. Worst case 257 calls per task.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 for a text-level selector: a pool-to-shortlist step by the model itself loses about a quarter of good hypotheses. Keep the pool and rank by code execution, do not let the model summarise it away.

source: Parab et al. (2025) Analysis of Error Sources in LLM-based Hypothesis Search (rescue analysis)
finding: Executing candidate programs against the examples rescues many trials where the front end failed. When generator and summariser both had a correct hypothesis, the implementor solved the test case almost always.
numbers: Both succeed: test solved in 95.9%. Generator ok, summariser failed: still 75.3%. Both failed: 1092 trials rescued, 37.0% of that subset and 19.9% of all trials. Generator success makes implementor success about 19 times more likely on train and 17 times on test (p<.001). Trial-level r=.57 train, .55 test; task-level r=.93 and .79.
limits: Same single-model setup. Train-to-test drop shows brittle train fits still happen.
agent_relevance: Execution is a stronger filter than text judgment. Generation of a good hypothesis stays the main bottleneck (so sample more diverse hypotheses), while selection by running code is cheap and works.

source: Xiong (2026) Hypothesis generation and updating in large language models
finding: In the number game, eight LLMs asked to pick a hypothesis from a shown list (evaluation) chose ones that fit the examples better than the hypotheses they generated freely. Free generation favoured narrower, rule-like hypotheses that fit less well.
numbers: Eight LLMs, non-thinking mode, TENENBAUM99 stimulus set with 100-number domain. Evaluation top-1 more consistent with examples than generation top-1; gap grows as examples accumulate. Single cached run per model, single seed.
quote: LLMs select more correct hypotheses during hypothesis evaluation but generate simpler, more rule-like hypotheses.
limits: Preprint. Number game only. Authors note the comparison is asymmetric by design (evaluation supplies candidates, generation requires search).
agent_relevance: Supports a two-step design: generate many candidates, then score a shown list against the examples. Models are better judges of a list than authors of the best hypothesis (gap 2, gap 8).

source: Xiong (2026) Hypothesis generation and updating in LLMs (prior, sampling and extrapolation)
finding: By default LLMs behave as if examples were sampled from the true concept (strong sampling), which gives a built-in preference for narrow hypotheses. Thinking mode and a weak-sampling prompt shift this toward the prior but do not remove it. Rule-versus-interval structure inside the examples collapses when the query lies outside them.
numbers: Two-parameter Bayesian fit; projection of prediction, evaluation and generation probes onto the same plane shows the three readouts do not agree. Extrapolation tested on the larger domain 101-200.
limits: Single seed per model. Prompts matter a lot; authors say results are a relative comparison under their reference model.
agent_relevance: For gap 8: a prompt that says the examples are incidental moves behaviour in the right direction, but the three probes disagree, so one prompt will not fix overgeneralisation or undergeneralisation everywhere. Score on held-out queries beyond the examples.

source: Bazigaran and Sohn (2025) Concept Generalization in Humans and Large Language Models: Insights from the Number Game
finding: GPT stays anchored to the one shown number after a single example, while humans and a Bayesian model spread to rule and similarity concepts. GPT needs several examples before its fit to the Bayesian model matches the human fit.
numbers: Mean pairwise JSD: human-Bayes lower than GPT-human and GPT-Bayes. GPT-Bayes divergence becomes comparable to human-Bayes at set length L=4; human-Bayes unaffected by length.
limits: One GPT model, figure-level quantities partly read from plots. No candidate-list prompt tested.
agent_relevance: Independent confirmation of one-example under-generalisation (gap 8). Practical rule: do not trust a single-example induction; ask for several candidate rules and keep them open until about four examples.

source: Wei et al. (2025) CodeARC: Benchmarking Reasoning Capabilities of LLM Agents for Inductive Program Synthesis
finding: The first function o3-mini wrote fitted the 10 given examples far more often than it was correct against a differential-testing oracle. Letting the agent query the hidden function for new inputs and use counterexamples raised success.
numbers: 1114 functions, 18 models, best o3-mini 52.7% success (59.5% annotated variant). First synthesised function: 67.6% pass the 10 initial examples, 38.9% pass the oracle, 28.7% (640 problems) fit the examples but are wrong. Success rises with more I/O budget and more oracle calls.
limits: Python functions; the oracle is differential testing (a strong verifier the agent usually lacks). Only the first attempt is counted for the 28.7% figure.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the fit-but-wrong rate for a strong reasoning model on general functions is about 29%, far above the 9% in K22. Holding examples out helps only if the agent can also ask for or generate new inputs. A counterexample search is worth more than extra fitting.

source: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats
finding: Study 1 crossed information format (probability vs frequency) with menu (standard: base rate, hit rate, false-alarm rate; short: joint counts). The frequency advantage holds within each menu, but the short menu alone also lifts probability-format performance.
numbers: Bayesian algorithms: frequency 46% (standard menu) and 50% (short menu); probability 16% (standard) and 28% (short). 15 problems, human students, protocol-based coding. Predictions: short menu helps probability format, not frequency format.
quote: Probability formats, in contrast, elicited 16% and 28%, for the standard menu and the short menu, respectively.
limits: Human students. Authors' own account is computational simplicity; rivals (nested sets) explain the same data differently.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 for humans: menu is not the whole effect (22 to 30 point format gap at fixed menu), but menu explains 12 of the 30 points on the probability side. For the agent, rewrite to the short menu of joint counts first. No LLM study crosses these two factors.

source: Neace, Michaud, Bolling, Deer, Zecevic (2008) Frequency formats, probability formats, or problem structure? A test of the nested-sets hypothesis
finding: Five experiments on the Linda problem. Earlier frequency benefits confounded format with having a concrete reference class and with the response type. With the confound removed, conjunction errors fall with a reference class in either format, and frequency formats are no better than probability formats.
numbers: Experiment 1 N=100 introductory psychology students (full tables not read).
limits: Conjunction task only, college students. Read abstract, introduction and general discussion; per-experiment percentages not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and gap 4: the useful part of a frequency rewrite is stating the reference class ('out of 100 women like Linda') and the nested sets, not the word frequency. Build that into the rewrite operator.

source: Yax, Anllo, Palminteri (2023, rev.) Studying and improving reasoning in humans and machines
finding: Wrote 1024 fresh Linda/Bill-form items (new names, jobs, domains) after finding the original Linda wording looked familiar to GPT-3 models. Older GPT-3 models were near chance; humans showed a Linda effect; chatGPT and especially GPT-4 were near ceiling on the fresh items.
numbers: Fresh items: 128 human and 128 model participants, 8 Linda and 8 Bill items each. GPT-3 pooled: Bill .53, Linda .46. Humans: Bill .83, Linda .56. chatGPT Linda .70 (Bill-Linda gap .12). GPT-4 Linda .98, Bill .99.
quote: GPT-4 displayed even higher performance, showing a correct response rate approaching to 100% for both items
limits: GPT-4 as of 2023 with two-option multiple choice; fresh items share the original structure, so a model could have learned the abstract form. Not tested: reversed items where the conjunction is true.
agent_relevance: Gap 4, partial answer: a 2023 frontier model passes fresh surface-different Linda items, so 'only the famous version' is too strong. K09 should be softened. Mutation with reversed logic (next lines) is the better probe.

source: Jiang, Xie, Hao, Wang, Mallick, Su, Taylor, Roth (2024) A Peek into Token Bias: Large Language Models Are Not Yet Genuine Reasoners
finding: Perturbed conjunction-fallacy problems with name swaps, celebrity names, irrelevant narrative and hint tokens and tested paired accuracy with McNemar tests. Almost all models rejected the genuine-reasoning null under some prompts. Swapping the exemplar name Linda for Bob lowered accuracy for all models tested.
numbers: Hypothesis 1 n=400, H2 n=500, H3 n=100. Models incl. gpt-3.5, gpt-4-turbo, gpt-4o, claude-3 opus and sonnet, llama-3, mistral-large. GPT-4o few-shot was near 100% and the null was not rejected there (p=0.159, 1 discordant pair). H2 e.g. gpt-4-turbo one-shot 110 vs 13 discordant pairs.
limits: Models are 2024 versions. Synthetic items generated by GPT-4. Paired tests need discordant pairs, so very strong settings give no power.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the mutation check (G3) is the right test, and the paired mutated-vs-original design can be copied directly. Failures were driven by irrelevant surface tokens, so strip them in a restatement step.

source: Williams et al. (2025) Frontier LLMs Still Struggle with Simple Reasoning Tasks (Unpuzzles)
finding: Built easy versions of famous puzzles by minimal edits. For the conjunctive fallacy the unpuzzle states that Linda is a feminist and asks which is more probable, bank teller or feminist (answer: feminist). o1 gave the classic problem's answer and called it the classic form.
numbers: Appendix D, Figures 15 and 16: o1 states that the correct answer is always option A to a changed problem where the correct answer is B.
limits: Only this worked example read in detail; the paper's overall accuracy on the Linda unpuzzle was not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a frontier reasoning model can fail a Linda-form item when the logic is flipped, which is exactly what a mutated-input check would catch. Add a flipped-logic variant to the G3 check.

source: Huang, Zhang, Kwak, An (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Benchmark of four bias families with computable baselines on three models. A prompt that tells the model to avoid bias fixed response biases but made judgment biases (including base-rate and probabilistic reasoning) slightly worse.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, T=0. Debiasing prompt: Response biases +40.5% position independence, Judgment -4.4% accuracy, information-processing negligible. Judgment bias rate 19.8% on average.
limits: Small open and mini-class models, not frontier. Judgment family pools base rate, anchoring, sunk cost and status quo, so base-rate alone is not separated.
agent_relevance: Supports K25: do not rely on a 'beware base rate' instruction. Pair it with computation (gap 1).

source: Pournemat et al. (2025) Reasoning Under Uncertainty: Exploring Probabilistic Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs
finding: Models lose track of counts as the context grows and do worse on conditional than joint distributions. Giving GPT-4.1-mini a code interpreter to count frequencies nearly closed the gap to a setting where the frequencies were handed over.
numbers: Accuracy drops with joint-space size; over 60% degradation with longer context. Interpreter run on GPT-4.1-mini (Appendix H) described as substantially improved, nearly matching the frequency-provided setting. Exact table not extracted.
limits: Not a Bayes word problem: tasks are mode finding, MLE and sampling over given counts. Single model for the code arm.
agent_relevance: Indirect evidence for gap 1: counting and conditioning are where prose reasoning degrades and code helps. No study runs the full extract-then-compute arm on base-rate vignettes, so gap 1 stays open and must be run in-house.

source: Dai, Teehan, Torabian, Ren (2026) Aligning LLMs with Human Uncertainty: A Beta-Bernoulli Calibrator for LLM Forecasting
finding: On 1614 held-out forecasting questions (resolved after the models' knowledge cutoffs), post-hoc Platt scaling of LLM verbalised probabilities cut Brier score for all four LLMs. Isotonic regression helped some models and badly hurt others.
numbers: Calibrator trained on 7,824 questions (validation 1,917). Claude-Sonnet-4 Brier: verbalised .146, Platt .129, isotonic .128. Llama-3.3-70B .157 to .138 (Platt) but isotonic .265. Qwen3-32B .158 to .137, Qwen3-8B .185 to .141. Human crowd Brier .061. AUC barely changes (.723 to .724), ECE .104 to .038.
limits: Platt is a two-parameter fit (slope and intercept), not the one-parameter power of K27. Trained on thousands of questions; the minimum data was not tested. The paper's learned calibrator did better still.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: recalibration fitted in code helps current LLMs, mostly by fixing overconfidence, not by better ranking. Data need is untested here; use a two-parameter fit only once there are hundreds of resolved items.

source: Wang, Deng, Yang (2026) Assessing and Mitigating Miscalibration in LLM-Based Social Science Measurement
finding: Platt and Beta scaling drive calibration error to near zero but leave Brier high, a sign the outputs collapse toward the base rate and lose resolution. Rank-preserving temperature scaling is recommended instead.
numbers: Platt and Beta reduce T-ECE often from above 0.400 to below 0.030 while Brier stays disproportionately high. 1,000-sample calibration subsets per construct. Some proprietary models severely miscalibrated (T-ECE 0.466, Brier 0.438).
limits: Classification-style measurement of text, not forecasting. Different task from the forecasting study.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: judge a recalibrator by Brier and resolution, not ECE alone. A fit that improves ECE but not Brier is a warning sign.

source: Li, Wang, Zheng, Song (2025) Patterns Over Principles: The Fragility of Inductive Reasoning in LLMs under Noisy Observations
finding: Built a Robust Rule Induction task where a share of seen examples are wrong. Method SRR samples diverse subsets of the examples, induces rules, and checks them by running code; it lost little accuracy under 10% noise while CoT, self-consistency and hypothesis refinement lost more. Accuracy alone hides instability: rules change even when accuracy does not.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3. SRR best in 10 of 14 task-model cells at 10% noise with 2.1% average accuracy gap. Tasks: base-7/8/9 addition, Caesar/Atbash/Keyboard ciphers, list functions. Consistency with clean-data answers can be 70% with 0% accuracy change.
limits: Noise is random output corruption, not subtle errors. The paper does not detect which example is bad; it votes across subsets. Table columns partly garbled in text extraction, so only the average gap is quoted.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: subset sampling plus code execution recovers most accuracy without finding the bad example. Cheap version: induce on several random subsets, keep the rule that fits the most examples, flag the examples it fails as suspects.

source: Rodriguez, Mueller, Misra (2025) Characterizing the Role of Similarity in the Property Inferences of Language Models
finding: With nonce-word properties, language models project a property more readily when the categories are taxonomically related and also similar; taxonomy and similarity both matter and are not separable.
numbers: 2,016 taxonomically related pairs; similarity from WordNet and SPoSE-based odd-one-out data. Behavioural and causal-representation analyses; exact accuracy table not extracted.
limits: Studies base language-model behaviour with likelihood scoring, not prompting with a taxonomy. Opened intro and method; results tables skimmed only.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: no study adds explicit taxonomy or causal structure to a prompt and compares with similarity-only at equal tokens. Models already carry some taxonomic bias, so the gain from naming the taxonomy may be small. Run it in-house.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors, Kemp (2024) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models (pragmatic account)
finding: Search snippet only: authors propose that people judge non-monotonic arguments weaker because they assume a helpful speaker chose the premises, and GPT-4 does not capture this.
numbers: Not re-opened this pass; see c01 to c05 for numbers.
limits: Snippet. No follow-up study that adds a 'why were these premises chosen' prompt was found in searches.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: untested whether a teacher-assumption prompt helps current models. Searches turned up no direct test.
